draft.title: Australia's system of government
card: Before 1901 each colony governed itself. At Federation the colonies became states and joined to form the Commonwealth of Australia. Power was shared between the Commonwealth and the states.
The Constitution is the written set of rules for this sharing. It lists what the Commonwealth parliament can make laws about, such as defence and trade with other countries.
The Commonwealth has three parts. The parliament makes laws, the government carries them out, and the courts, including the High Court, decide disputes about the law and the Constitution.
The states kept their own parliaments. The NSW Parliament still makes laws on state matters, such as public schools and public hospitals.
draft.remember: The Constitution shares power between the Commonwealth and the states, and each has its own parliament.

a.q: What does the Constitution do in Australia's system of government?
opts: Sets out how power is shared between the Commonwealth and states
Gives all law-making power to the Commonwealth parliament
Replaces the state parliaments with one national parliament
Lets the High Court make the laws for each state
a.why: The Constitution is the written set of rules that shares power between the Commonwealth and the states. It does not give the Commonwealth all power, because the states kept their own parliaments.
a.clue: Think about what was shared at Federation, and what the states kept.

b.q: A student in Newcastle asks who makes laws about the running of her public high school. Which answer is correct?
opts: The NSW Parliament, because schools are a state matter
The High Court, because it decides disputes about laws
The Commonwealth parliament, because it makes all laws
The Constitution, because it makes the laws itself
b.why: The states kept their own parliaments for state matters such as public schools, so the NSW Parliament makes these laws. The Commonwealth parliament does not make all laws, only those the Constitution allows.
b.clue: Which parliament did NSW keep for state matters?
